idiom_name: reference semantics + final class with no copy constructor and no Cloneable
implementation_notes: Java classes are reference types: assignment copies a reference and no copy constructor is generated, so the classic mixin has nothing to suppress and the pattern degenerates into a declaration discipline - make the class `final` (otherwise a subclass can add state or copying), keep the constructor private and construct through static factories, do not implement `Cloneable`, and do not write a copy constructor unless copying is genuinely part of the contract. `Object.clone()` is protected and throws `CloneNotSupportedException` unless the class opts in via `Cloneable`, and the JDK documentation recommends copy constructors or static factories over `Cloneable` for new classes, so the remaining work is refusing the opt-in (and keeping it refused). The classic base-class form is still justified for the inverse problem - a value type that stays usable as a value but must reject cloning: an abstract base that overrides `clone()` to throw is the only mechanism Java offers.
pitfalls: `Cloneable` is a marker interface without a `clone()` method: implementing it changes nothing at compile time but makes Object.clone() perform a field-for-field copy at runtime, and arrays always look Cloneable - never implement it on an identity type.
`final` alone is not enough if someone later adds `Cloneable` or a copy constructor; the guarantee is only as stable as the class's public API, so record the reason in the javadoc.
Serialisation (`Serializable`) and frameworks that reconstruct objects by reflection bypass the private constructor, so a serialiser can still materialise a second instance.
Reflection and low-level allocation can always make another instance: Java's guarantee is API-level, not type-system-level, so use immutability for anything security-relevant.
